Middle Ear 3-D Transplant - A World First!

By: Mart-Marie Faure | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
World's first middle ear transplant pioneered by a South African academic.

Unique Selling Point:
A pioneering surgical procedure using 3D-printed middle ear bones, developed by Professor Mashudu Tshifularo and his team at the University of Pretoria Faculty of Health, may be the answer to conductive hearing loss, a middle ear problem caused by congenital birth defects, infection, trauma or metabolic loss.


Summary:
The surgery which can be performed on everyone including newborns. On March 13 Prof Tshifularo will perform a transplant surgery on a patient with damaged middle ear bones due to an accident and having suffered meningitis. replacing the hammer, anvil and stirrup, the bones that make up the middle ear. 3D Printing is used to print these bones.
The procedure carries less risk than known prostheses and their associated surgical procedures. Titanium is used which is biocompatible. An endoscope is used to do the replacement and the scarring is minimal. The surgery also aims to simplify the reconstruction of bones during middle ear procedures. The procedure reduces the chance of facial nerve paralysis, which can occur if the facial nerve that passes through the middle ear space is damaged during traditional surgery.


Further information:
The 3D printed bones were designed and manufactured by three remarkable men.
Jason Laing is a Bio-material specialist and a jeweler by trade. Four years ago he was seriously injured in a cycle accident.
He had 32 broken bones and suffered serious head injuries. Doctors had very little hope of recovery but Jason teamed up with Gavin Leggot, a 3D manufacturing engineer and Philip vd Walt, a medical product designer. They designed and developed 3D printed bones to replace the seriously damaged bones in Jason's body enabling him to recover and live a normal life.
Professor Mashudu Tshifularo, pioneer and innovator, from the Ear, Nose and Throat Department at the University of Pretoria, had been searching for a way to realize his middle ear invention for the past ten years. Two years ago he read about Jason and got hold of the trio on their website. Together they developed the 3D-printed titanium bones.
